notes.title: Start here: six traced flows through Umami
notes.body:
Umami is a privacy-focused, open-source web analytics app (Next.js, Prisma, optional ClickHouse, Redis and Kafka). The study track is `umami/fabledocs/upskill/`.

Read in this order:

1. `01-codebase-cartography/05-key-flows.md`: six flows (collection, an authorized read, login, pixel and link tracking, session replay, public sharing), each with a numbered trace table.
2. `03-architecture-and-patterns/03-validation-auth-and-permissions.md` for where validation, authentication and authorization happen.
3. `03-architecture-and-patterns/04-side-effects-async-and-reliability.md` for writes and failure modes.

Paths in the tables are under `umami/src/`. Collection endpoints live under `src/app/api/send`, `src/app/api/record` and `src/app/(collect)/`.

Each table row compresses several lines of code. For every row the quiz touches, open the file at the cited line and read the surrounding branch. The guide was written against an earlier read of the code, and a couple of rows no longer match the file exactly; when they disagree, the file wins.

notes.title: Concept: unauthenticated collection and hashed identity
notes.body:
Umami collects page views without cookies. The browser script sends a JSON payload to `POST /api/send`, which has no login at all (`skipAuth: true`). Two ideas make this work.

**Identity by hashing.** Instead of storing a visitor id, the server derives one: `uuid(...args)` in `src/lib/crypto.ts` hashes its arguments together with a server secret into a deterministic UUID. The same inputs always give the same id. Read which inputs the send handler passes, under which condition it passes different ones, and how `getSalt` turns a date into a salt for each rotation setting.

**A signed client-side cache.** The response includes a signed token that the tracker sends back as `x-umami-cache`, letting the server skip work on later requests.

Read `src/app/api/send/route.ts` from `POST` to the visit logic and list every early `return` in order, with what it returns. Then do the same for `src/app/api/record/route.ts`, and look at how the pixel route in `src/app/(collect)/p/[slug]/route.ts` records its hit.

readMore.why: The collection handler: schema, cache token, identity and the write.

notes.title: Concept: authenticate, then authorize
notes.body:
Dashboard routes follow a two-step shape. `parseRequest` in `src/lib/request.ts` validates the input with Zod and calls `checkAuth`; the route handler then calls a permission function such as `canViewWebsite` in `src/permissions/website.ts`. Keep the two words apart: authentication answers "who is this?", authorization answers "may they see this website?".

Things to trace:

- In `parseRequest`, the order of validation and authentication, and the condition under which `checkAuth` runs at all.
- In `checkAuth` (`src/lib/auth.ts`), the two ways a request can be accepted (a bearer token or a share token) and every path that returns `null`. Note which request headers each path reads.
- In `canViewWebsite`, the order of its checks and what it does for a website owned by a team.
- In `src/app/api/auth/login/route.ts`, how a failed login is answered, and how the two token strategies are chosen. Read `saveAuth` and note its parameters and their defaults.

excerpts.quote: authenticate in `parseRequest`, then authorize with an explicit `can*` call in the handler.

notes.title: Why an unknown website id gets 400
notes.body:
With no cached `websiteId`, the handler calls `fetchWebsite(websiteId)`. It returns null for a missing or soft-deleted website, and the handler answers `badRequest({ message: 'Website not found.' })`, which `src/lib/response.ts` builds with status 400. The guide's trace table says 404 for this step; the code returns 400.

- *404 from fetchWebsite*: fetchWebsite returns null; the handler chooses badRequest.
- *200 beep boop*: that is the bot response, which comes later.
- *401*: collection has no authentication.

notes.title: Why bots get beep boop before the IP block
notes.body:
After client info is resolved, the handler checks `!process.env.DISABLE_BOT_CHECK && isbot(userAgent)` and returns `json({ beep: 'boop' })`, a 200. Only after that does it check `hasBlockedIp(ip)` and return 403. A bot from a blocked IP therefore gets the 200 body, and nothing is written.

- *403 first*: the IP check comes second in the file.
- *400 from Zod*: the user agent is not part of the schema.
- *Stored with a cache token*: the handler returns before any session or event write.

notes.title: How a payload id changes the session id
notes.body:
`sessionId = id ? uuid(sourceId, id) : uuid(sourceId, ip, userAgent, sessionSalt)`. With an id, only the website (or pixel or link) id and the supplied id are hashed, so the IP, user agent and salt do not matter and the same id on any device yields the same session. `uuid` with arguments is a v5 UUID of their hash plus the server secret.

- *Same as without id*: the ternary picks a different argument list.
- *Random v4*: v4 or v7 is used only when uuid is called with no arguments.
- *uuid(id, ip)*: the source id is always included and the IP is not.

excerpts.quote: const sessionId = id ? uuid(sourceId, id) : uuid(sourceId, ip, userAgent, sessionSalt);

notes.title: Why sessions roll over monthly by default
notes.body:
The handler reads `process.env.SALT_ROTATION || 'month'`. `getSalt` uses `startOfDay` for day, `startOfWeek` for week and `startOfMonth` otherwise, and hashes that date. With the default, the same IP and user agent give the same session id for the whole calendar month. The guide's row mentions a day; the code's default is a month.

- *A single day*: only when SALT_ROTATION is day.
- *One hour*: the hourly salt (`visitSalt`) is for visit ids.
- *Forever*: a salt is always mixed in.

notes.title: Why a bad query wins over a missing token
notes.body:
`parseRequest` runs `schema.safeParse` first. On failure it sets `error` to a `badRequest`. Authentication is guarded by `!options?.skipAuth && !error`, so once validation has failed `checkAuth` is not called and the route returns the 400.

- *401 first*: authentication runs only after a successful parse.
- *403*: parseRequest never produces 403; permission checks happen later in the handler.
- *200 with a log*: the error is returned to the route, which returns it.

notes.title: Why an empty replay batch needs no token
notes.body:
The schema allows an empty `events` array (it only caps the length at 200). Immediately after parsing, the route returns `json({ ok: true })` when `!events?.length`. The session-token check comes after that, so an empty batch is accepted without a token.

- *Missing session token*: that check is never reached for an empty batch.
- *Zod requires an event*: the schema sets a maximum, not a minimum.
- *403*: no authorization or billing check has run yet.

notes.title: Why replay needs the collection token
notes.body:
A non-empty batch requires the `x-umami-cache` header. Without it, the route returns `badRequest({ message: 'Missing session token.' })`. Replay never creates a session itself; it attaches chunks to the session and visit that collection already established.

- *New session created*: the replay route has no session-creation code.
- *401*: skipAuth is set, so there is no authentication step to fail.
- *replay_disabled*: that response comes after the token check, when the website flag is off.

notes.title: What a disabled replay returns
notes.body:
With a valid token, the route loads the website with `getWebsite` directly (the comment says this avoids a stale Redis copy of the flag). If `replayEnabled` is false it returns `json({ ok: false, reason: 'replay_disabled' })`, a 200 with a reason, and stores nothing.

- *403 business subscription*: that CLOUD_MODE check runs only for websites with replay on.
- *Website not found*: the website exists.
- *ok true and stored*: the route returns before saving.

notes.title: Why a share token alone is refused
notes.body:
`checkAuth` parses the bearer token and the share token. With no user and a share token, it reads the share-context header; if that header is missing it logs "Share token used outside share context" and returns null. `parseRequest` turns null into 401. Share tokens therefore work only from requests that also send the context header, as the share pages do.

- *Auth with shareToken*: that is returned only when the context header is present.
- *Auth for the share's creator*: share tokens carry granted ids, not a user.
- *Throws*: the function returns null; nothing throws.

excerpts.quote: log('Share token used outside share context');

notes.title: Why a non-member cannot view a team website
notes.body:
`canViewWebsite` returns true for admins and for share tokens that list the id. Otherwise it loads the entity. A team-owned website has `teamId` set, so the function returns `!!teamUser` from `getTeamUser(entity.teamId, user.id)`, which is false when the user is not on the team.

- *Any signed-in user*: ownership or membership is required.
- *Team websites readable by all*: only members pass.
- *Throws a 403*: the function returns a boolean, and the route decides the response.

notes.title: Why both failed logins look the same
notes.body:
The login route evaluates `!user || !checkPassword(password, user.password)` as one condition and returns `unauthorized({ code: 'incorrect-username-password' })`. An unknown username and a wrong password produce the same 401 body, so an attacker cannot use the response to learn which usernames exist.

- *404 for an unknown user*: that would reveal which names exist.
- *403 for a wrong password*: both cases use unauthorized.
- *400 field error*: both requests pass the schema (two strings).

notes.title: Why the Redis login key has no TTL
notes.body:
`saveAuth(data, expire = 0)` writes the key with `redis.client.set` and calls `expire` only `if (expire)`. The login route calls `saveAuth({ userId: id, role })` with one argument, so expire is 0 and the key has no TTL. It stays until something deletes it; because it lives server-side, deleting it revokes the session.

- *24 hours*: the default is 0, which means no expiry call.
- *7 days*: no expiry is set on this path.
- *30 minutes*: that is the visit window in collection, unrelated to login.

excerpts.quote: export async function saveAuth(data: any, expire = 0) {
token = await saveAuth({ userId: id, role });

notes.title: How the pixel route reuses collection
notes.body:
After resolving the pixel by slug, the route builds a payload `{ type: 'event', payload: { pixel: pixel.id, url, referrer } }`, wraps it in a new POST `Request` that reuses the inbound headers (so IP and user agent carry over), and calls `await POST(req)` from the send route. Then it returns the 1x1 GIF with no-cache headers.

- *Prisma insert directly*: the route writes nothing itself.
- *Kafka without waiting*: it awaits the send handler, and Kafka is only one possible backend of saveEvent.
- *Redirect to /api/send*: a redirect is what the link route does to its target URL, not to the API.
